title: Ramana at sixteen: who am I?
hook: a sixteen-year-old lies down on the floor as if dead, and asks what dies
carry: atman: the one the thoughts come to
tomorrow: how can someone work in the world and not get stained?

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti: the saints who sang to God in the language of home. Today, the modern teachers.

Madurai, in south India, 1896. A schoolboy of sixteen named Venkataraman is alone in an upstairs room of his uncle's house. He isn't ill. But, as he later told it, a sudden, overwhelming fear of death comes over him. He doesn't run for help. He lies down, stretches out stiff like a corpse, holds his breath, and asks himself: this body is dead. They'll carry it to the burning ground. But am I dead?
screen: `MADURAI, 1896. A BOY OF SIXTEEN.` → `HE LIES DOWN AS IF DEAD.` → `BUT AM I DEAD?`

segments.voice: His answer, as he later told it, didn't come as an argument. The body lay still, and he felt himself fully alive, untouched by its death. About six weeks later he left home for the holy hill of Arunachala, at Tiruvannamalai, and he stayed there the rest of his life. People came from everywhere to sit with him, and called him Ramana Maharshi. His teaching was the question that boy asked on the floor: who am I? It is one of the oldest teachings in Hinduism, made small enough to carry. The Upanishads call it atman: the Self, the one who sees, which is not the body and not the thoughts. In Advaita Vedanta, the school Ramana's teaching is usually placed in, atman is one with Brahman. His short text Who Am I? turns it into a practice, self-inquiry. Thoughts will keep coming. Don't chase them, and don't fight them. When one arrives, ask: to whom has this come? To me. Then: who am I? The mind, he says, turns back toward its source, and the thought falls quiet. In the end the questioning itself burns up, like the stick used to stir a funeral fire. The question isn't a riddle with an answer like I am this body. It turns attention around, from what appears to the one it appears to. The other modern teachers carried old paths into new rooms too: Vivekananda opened in Chicago with "Sisters and Brothers of America"; Gandhi read the Gita as a guide to action; Tagore made prayer into Gitanjali. Ramana carried it into one question.
screen: `FULLY ALIVE. THEN, ARUNACHALA.` · `WHO AM I? ATMAN: THE SELF.` · `THOUGHTS COME. ASK: TO WHOM?` · `TO ME. WHO AM I?` · then, large: `TURN ATTENTION AROUND.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, and when a thought arrives, neither follow it nor push it away; ask quietly, to whom did this come? To me. Then ask, who am I? Don't answer in words: let attention turn back toward the one who is asking, and rest there until the next thought comes.
Ramana. The boy of sixteen who asked what dies, and whose whole path fits in one question: who am I?
Your line: atman: the one the thoughts come to. Tomorrow, a lotus leaf. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-inquiry by asking "who am I?" whenever thoughts arise, in sitting practice and in daily life, and many visit his ashram at Arunachala in Tiruvannamalai; Vivekananda's addresses and Tagore's Gitanjali are read and recited widely.
